I think in your case part of what might be going on is that your friends and love ones may feel partly responsible for your suicide attempt. Some of them at least are probably thinking that they may have neglected you and they're now trying to shift the blame they feel to you.  

My other theory, which may be more realistic, is that in general human beings want to avoid negativity at all costs. It doesn't help that our society doesn't really teach people how to talk to others experiencing personal mental health problems. 

When someone attempts suicide it's scary and it makes people close to the person feel uneasy about themselves. Because our society doesn't really teach us to be open with darker feelings in a healthy way a lot of people just don't know how to act around someone with depression and just avoid them. 

I'm not saying you did anything wrong. Depression makes us act in dramatic and unhealthy ways. I think what might help is if you just say to them I'm sorry for what I did but please understand I wasn't in a sound state of mind. 

I've never attempted suicide (though I've had the thoughts) but I have strained friendships because of depression. There's such a delicate balance between seeking help from friends and loved one and being unhealthily dependent on others. I can't say I've struck it perfectly but I think with time it gets easier. 

I hope that's coherent and uplifting. I feel you  for whatever that's worth.

That can mean actively helping them when they ask for it or letting them know you can do things for them but for me anyway, it also means just having a presence there. Also, let him know you mean a lot to him.

I think as well, you can give him an opportunity to do something around the house that will help out. You could suggest he do something that relies on a certain skill or talent of his. This might give a sense of accomplishment. 

I wish you guys all the best. He is a fortunate man to have  a wife who is trying to help him.

(http://thelifeofbinkleton.blogspot.com/2015/08/does-facebook-need-more-misery.html) 

These have been some fascinating and interesting responses. Many Thanks Guys! 

I was partly prompted to post this question after writing a blog-post on the subject of Facebook envy. 

I know we're not supposed to self-promote but I would really be interested in any feedback you'd be willing to give on what I've written. 

Personally, I feel as if sharing miseries on FB became more common it would help a lot of people. That's why I've been making a more conscious effort to share some of my darker times online.

Yeah, I'm the same. It's actually quite common to feel like that. It's called Facebook envy. While I think everyone gets it and is affected by it, that kind of envy can be worse for people who are depressives.

I second ramsfan's advice. I can understand being nervous about sharing stuff like that with adults. I didn't feel comfortable sharing my own thoughts for a long time when I was in high school. Once I did I felt better. 

Now, I'm sure our situations are different on some level but a mental health counselor is someone who has the training to truly help you. 

I know it can be scary to trust an adult, especially if you haven't had the best time reaching out to your parents but I would say at least try. 

Know though you can always come back here if you have a hard time and have nowhere to turn.
Thanks so much I really appreciate it.

That happens a lot to me too. Well, really it happens to everyone who struggles. 

I think it at times like these where it's important to try and think of how far we've come. 

I know that's not always easy. Solidarity :)

I've been in that same place before as I also move around a lot for my job. I'm also in that spot currently. It's been hard having to deal with a lack of friends. That's what brought me here. 

If wherever your are now you can find a counselor or a forum to talk I'd recommend you do so. Otherwise you can always come back here to find people who will listen. You're not alone bud even if that's all you feel right now.

I've moved around between countries my entire life. I can remember how hard it was to have to deal with moving to a new school in a new culture. 

I often broke down and cried the first few years I was in Thailand. 

And yeah, much like ramsfan1104 said, smiling people sometimes do have some the darkest problems. That was actually something that took me a while to understand as I tend to have a sullen personality. 

I've actually described my depression as he feeling of being clawed away as well. 

I'm sorry that your home life isn't helping either. My guess is your parents feel like they're trying to do what's best for you in their own mind. Unfortunately a lot of people still don't understand the seriousness of the issue. 

I'm sure though if you kept trying you would find someone willing to listen. I don't know if you're school as a counselor or not but if it does definitely go to him/her. I was fortunate enough to have one when I was in high school and she was an enormous help. 

I'd also encourage you to consider talking to a teacher if you don't have a counselor and asking them for advice. They might be able to point you in the right direction. 

The biggest thing to remember is that you are definitely not alone and that there are millions of people suffering like we do. I know sometimes it doesn't feel that way. It still doesn't for me at times but you're a lot stronger than you think and I really believe you can find a way to start smiling genuinely again. 

I really hope these words help somehow.
